transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just can't seem to keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore. And it's really starting to scare me, to be honest, because it happens even when the work is incredibly important and people are relying on me. 

I'm a computer support specialist, and I've been doing this a long time—I have a graduate degree, I know my systems inside and out. But lately, I'll sit down to do something critical, like tracing a client's network problem. You know, they'll call in, their system is down, it's a high-priority ticket, the kind of thing you really need to drill down into right that second. So I'll pull up the diagnostic logs, which I've looked at a million times in my career, and I'll start reading. 

And then... I don't know, ten minutes will just vanish, and I'll suddenly snap to and realize I've reread the exact same block of log entries three times. Three times! And I still don't even know what they say. It's like the text and the timestamps are just passing right through my vision without actually registering in my brain. I just sit there staring at the screen, knowing I need to fix this network issue, knowing the client is waiting, but my focus just completely evaporates before I can actually get to the bottom of the problem. It's just incredibly frustrating to know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing and just... not be able to hold my attention on it long enough to actually do it.
Does this difficulty with focusing happen only when you're working or do you also find it hard to concentrate on other things, like hobbies or conversations?

Well, like I was saying, it's really the work stuff that brought me in today, because that's what's scaring me the most. I mean, I just can't keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore, even when it's incredibly important. Like I mentioned with the network logs... I'll start tracing a client's problem, and it's a high-priority ticket, right? The kind of thing where every minute counts. And I'll pull up the logs, and I'll start reading, and then... it's just gone. Ten minutes will pass, and I'll realize I've reread the exact same block of log entries three times. Three times! And I still don't even know what they say. It's just... it's like my brain just refuses to hold onto the information, no matter how hard I try to force it. So, yeah, it's really the work tasks, those important things that I just can't seem to stay focused on long enough to actually get them done.
Do you have trouble focusing on things when you're not working?

Actually, yes. Now that you ask... I know I've been harping on the work stuff, because that's my livelihood, but it really bleeds into everything else, too. Especially the downtime, which is almost more frustrating in a way, because downtime is supposed to be easy, right? You're just supposed to relax. But I can't. 

Take anything quiet that should theoretically relax me. Like sitting through a movie with my wife. She knows how stressed I've been with these network tickets, so she'll try to set up a nice, relaxing evening for us. We'll sit down on the couch, put something on, and I really do want to watch it with her. I want to just be present. But I swear, we get maybe a few minutes into the film, and I just... I can't just sit there. My skin starts feeling tight, and before I know it, I'm pulling out my phone to check my emails or look up random trivia about where the movie was filmed. And I'll start muttering comments out loud about the plot holes or the lighting, just talking to myself, really, until she has to pause the TV. And half the time, I end up just getting up from the couch entirely. I'll walk into the kitchen, open the fridge, stare at the mustard, and walk back. For absolutely no real reason! I wasn't even hungry or thirsty. 

And it's the same with anything quiet. If I try to sit in my armchair and read a manual—even for a piece of tech I bought for myself, just for fun—I'm doing the exact same thing. Up and down, checking my phone, losing my place. My wife even suggested I try one of those breathing exercises. She downloaded an app for me, the kind where a calm voice tells you to breathe in for four seconds, hold it, exhale... I tried it to humor her, I really did. But I make it maybe two or three minutes before I'm opening my eyes, checking the timer on the phone to see how much longer I have to sit there in silence, and just muttering about how ridiculous the whole thing feels. I just can't seem to tolerate quiet activities anymore without jumping out of my skin.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're sitting still?

Oh, constantly. It's actually a bit embarrassing at my age, to be perfectly honest with you. You'd think a fifty-three-year-old man with a graduate degree would know how to sit still in a chair, but I just... I can't. 

I'll be sitting there with a client, right? Maybe we're going over a new server deployment, or I'm trying to explain why their firewall is blocking their own internal emails, which is a whole other headache we don't need to get into. But I'm sitting at their nice, expensive conference table, trying to project this calm, authoritative professional image. But underneath the table? My leg is just going a mile a minute. Just bouncing, bouncing, bouncing like a jackhammer. 

And if it's not my leg, it's my hands. My hands always have to be doing something. I'll grab whatever is nearby—usually a pen—and I just start clicking it. Click, click, click. Or, because I'm in IT, I almost always have these little plastic cable ties in my pockets, you know, zip ties? I'll pull one out without even thinking about it and just start turning it over and over in my fingers, bending it, twisting it around the tip of my thumb. 

And it's not just at work, either. I go to this local chess meeting on Thursday nights. Chess is supposed to be this deeply intellectual, still, focused game, right? You sit there in silence, you calculate variations. But I'll be sitting across the board from some guy who's taking fifteen minutes to make a single move, and I'm practically vibrating out of my seat. I'm bouncing my leg so hard I'm shaking the table, or I'm rolling a captured piece around in my palm. 

And the worst part is, I don't even realize I'm doing it! I have absolutely no idea I'm making all this noise or motion until... well, until somebody finally gives me *that look*. You know the look. The client will stop mid-sentence and just stare pointedly at the cable tie in my hands, or the guy at the chess club will sigh real loud and glare at my knee. And then I freeze, and I get all flushed, and I apologize and put my hands flat on the table. But I swear to you, five minutes later, I've picked up a paperclip or a coaster and I'm right back at it. It's like this physical energy just has to leak out of me somehow, and if I force myself to sit completely still, that feeling of jumping out of my skin just gets ten times worse.
Do you often act on impulse without fully thinking through the consequences?

Impulse? Acting on impulse? You know, I... I don't really think so. I mean, I'm an IT specialist, right? My whole job, my entire career, is built on logic and procedures and following the correct sequence of operations. You don't just impulsively reboot a primary domain controller in the middle of a workday, you know? You have to plan it out, schedule the downtime, notify the stakeholders. So, in that sense, no, I don't just do things without thinking about what's going to happen next. 

Even outside of work, I wouldn't say I'm an impulsive guy. Like with the chess club I mentioned. You can't be impulsive in chess. If you just grab a knight and toss it out there without calculating the lines, you're going to get crushed. You have to sit there and think, 'If I go here, he goes there, then I go there.' Now, I might be bouncing my leg under the table while I'm doing that calculation, like I said before, but I'm still doing the calculation. I'm not just making wild, thoughtless moves. 

I mean, sure, maybe I'll buy a new gadget or a tool without agonizing over the reviews for three weeks, but that's just because I know what I like, not because I'm out of control. I don't go out and buy a sports car on a whim, or, you know, quit my job because I had a bad Tuesday. I'm fifty-three, I have a mortgage, I have a wife. I think things through. I might get frustrated, I might get restless, and I might lose my train of thought when I'm trying to read those network logs, but I don't just... jump into things blindly. That's really not me. I try to be very deliberate, even if my brain feels like it's running a million miles an hour in a million different directions. The actions themselves? No, those are thought out. At least, I try my best to make sure they are.
Have you always had difficulty with focusing and restlessness, or is this something that has developed over time?

Oh, no, it is definitely not a new thing. Not at all. If anything, it has just sort of morphed as I got older. But the core of it? The restlessness and the focus issues? That has been there since day one. 

My mother actually still jokes about it to this day, which, you know, is a little grating when you are a fifty-three-year-old man, but she means well. She loves bringing up my old grade school report cards whenever we have family dinners. Every single one of them, without fail, had the exact same comments written in the margins by my teachers. They would always say I was a bright kid—which I was, I always understood the material just fine—but then they would write that I absolutely never stayed in my seat. It was like I was physically incapable of just sitting at a little wooden desk for forty-five minutes at a time. I was always up sharpening a pencil or looking out the window. 

And they would write that I constantly blurted out answers, too. I would never raise my hand. The teacher would ask a math question, and before she even finished the sentence, I would just shout out the number because my brain had already jumped to the end and I just could not hold the thought in my head. I had to get it out immediately. 

But the absolute worst part, the thing that drove my parents completely up the wall, was the homework. The report cards always mentioned me losing my homework. And the kicker is, I actually did it! I really did. I would sit at the kitchen table, do the worksheets, put them in my folder, put the folder in my backpack... and then the next morning, the teacher would ask to collect it, and it was just gone. Vanished into thin air. I would be digging frantically through my bag, pulling out crumpled up permission slips from three months ago and old candy wrappers, but the homework I had literally just done the night before? Nowhere to be found. 

So, yeah, it has always been exactly like this. It is not some mid-life crisis thing where I suddenly forgot how to concentrate. It is just... back then it was losing spelling worksheets and jumping out of my tiny classroom desk, and now it is losing track of network logs and bouncing my leg under a fancy corporate conference table. It is the exact same story, just a different setting, you know?
Do you feel like your difficulties with focusing and restlessness are interfering with your relationships or daily life?

Interfering? Yeah. Yeah, it’s... it’s doing a lot more than just interfering, to be perfectly honest with you. It feels like it's actively dismantling things right now. 

See, I used to have this very structured corporate setup. I had a project manager who basically wrangled my schedule, I had daily stand-up meetings, I had a ticketing system that dictated exactly what I was doing hour by hour. But since losing the structure of my old job, things have just completely unraveled. My reputation, which I’ve spent literally decades building in the IT sector, has taken a real hit. I’ve been trying to bridge the gap by taking on freelance clients—doing independent network consulting, server migrations, that sort of thing—but I just... I drop the ball. I miss the follow-up emails, or I get so restless and scattered during the initial consultations that I can see them losing confidence in me right there in the room. I’ve lost several good, paying freelance clients recently just because I couldn't keep my focus long enough to deliver what I promised on time.

And it's not just the freelance stuff. I was actually up for this senior service-manager role a couple of months ago. I was perfect for it on paper, you know? Graduate degree, years of hands-on experience. But the interview process required this massive, multi-stage mock deployment plan, and I just couldn't sit down and focus on the documentation. I kept getting up, pacing around the house, bouncing my leg at the desk, completely unable to string my thoughts together into a coherent project timeline. I missed the deadline for the submission, so obviously, I missed out on the role entirely. 

And the ripple effect of all this... well, it hits home. Literally. My wife and I have had to sit down at the kitchen table and seriously worry about money, which is terrifying when you're fifty-three and supposed to be in your peak earning years. It’s humiliating, frankly. We're looking at the mortgage and the bills, and she's stressed, and I'm stressed, and the absolute worst part of it all is that it just boils down to trust. People don’t trust me to follow through anymore. Not the clients, not the hiring managers... and sometimes I worry my wife is starting to feel the same way. I say I’ll do something, I have every intention of doing it, but then the focus just evaporates, and it doesn't get done. It's like watching a train wreck in slow motion, you know? You know exactly what you need to do to stop it, but you just can't make yourself do it, and then you have to make the phone call to apologize, and you sound like a flake. And in my industry, if you're a flake, you're dead in the water. So, yeah. It is definitely interfering.
Do you feel like your difficulties with focusing and restlessness are affecting your overall well-being or quality of life?

Well, yeah, I mean... it’s exactly like I was just saying a minute ago, but even deeper than just the daily logistics of it all. It is absolutely tanking my well-being. My quality of life is... well, it's pretty much in the gutter right now. Because, like I mentioned, ever since losing the structure of my old job, my reputation has taken such a massive, very real hit. And that doesn't just stay at work, you know? It follows you home. It gets inside your head and just sets up camp there.

When I think about how I’ve lost those freelance clients recently, or how I completely missed out on that senior service-manager role because I couldn't pull the documentation together... it’s not just a missed paycheck. It’s a massive blow to my ego, to my entire sense of self-worth. I’ve been a respected professional in the IT field for decades, and now I wake up every single morning with this huge pit in my stomach, just this overwhelming, exhausting dread. 

My wife and I, we’re constantly having to worry about money now, and let me tell you, financial stress at fifty-three is a completely different beast than when you're twenty-five and eating ramen. It ages you. It keeps you up at night staring at the ceiling. We should be planning for retirement, not agonizing over whether we can float the mortgage this month. 

And the absolute worst part for my mental well-being—the thing that really just ruins any chance of me having a good day—is knowing exactly why it's happening. It’s because people just don’t trust me to follow through anymore. That realization, that you are no longer seen as a reliable person by your peers or even your own spouse... it is completely devastating. It just eats away at you. You try to relax on a weekend, maybe sit down and watch a movie or something, but you can't, because your brain is just playing a highlight reel of all the people you've let down and the deadlines you've blown. You just feel entirely incapable. So, yes, my overall well-being is completely overshadowed by all of this. I just don't feel like the competent man I used to be, and that is a terrible, terrible way to live day in and day out.
Did you experience significant difficulties with focus, restlessness, or impulsivity as a child?

Yeah, like I—like I was mentioning earlier, when we first started talking, it was absolutely there when I was a kid. I mean, my mother still jokes about it to this day. We'll be at a holiday dinner or something, and she'll just launch right into it, bringing up those old grade school report cards for everyone to hear. 

Because year after year, every single one of those report cards said the exact same thing. The teachers would always make a point to write that I was a bright kid—which I was, I grasped the concepts just fine and the actual learning part wasn't the issue—but then they’d fill the margins with notes about how I absolutely never stayed in my seat. I was always up, always wandering around the classroom, totally unable to just sit still like the other kids. 

And they’d always write about how I constantly blurted out answers, too. I just couldn't raise my hand and wait my turn. The teacher would be halfway through a question, and the answer would just fly out of my mouth because I couldn't hold it in. And then, of course, there was the homework situation. My mom loves reminding me about how I’d constantly lose my assignments, which used to make me so frustrated because I actually *had* done it! I’d sit at the table, do all the work, pack it away, and then the next day... poof. Gone. Couldn't find it to turn it in. 

So, yes, to answer your question, all of that restlessness and trouble with focusing was very, very present back then. It’s been the exact same pattern since I was in elementary school, really.
Did you act on impulse a lot when you were a child?

Well, right, like I was literally just saying a second ago with the report cards... it's funny you use the word impulse, because when my mother makes those jokes about me blurting out answers—which, again, she does at basically every family gathering, Thanksgiving, you name it, it's her favorite story to tell—that’s exactly what it was. Pure impulse. 

I wasn't trying to be a bad kid or a show-off, you know? It wasn't malicious. It was just this... this immediate short-circuit between my brain and my mouth. The teacher—I remember Mrs. Gable in third grade especially, lovely woman but she had zero patience for me—she would be halfway through a math problem on the chalkboard, and the answer would just launch out of my mouth before I even registered that I hadn't raised my hand. I couldn't hold it in. It felt like a physical pressure in my chest that just had to get out.

And the same goes for never staying in my seat, which was the other big thing written in the margins of those report cards every single year. I wouldn't sit there and consciously decide, "I'm going to get up and walk around now." I'd just suddenly realize I was standing by the pencil sharpener, or wandering over to the window because a garbage truck drove by, and the teacher would be snapping her fingers at me to sit back down. My brain would just get a whim, and my legs would move before I could even think about the rules. 

Even losing the homework, which I know sounds more like just being disorganized, but it was driven by impulse too. I'd finish it, right? I'd sit at the kitchen table and actually do the work because, like the teachers always made a point to say, I was a bright kid. The concepts were easy for me. But then, the second I was done, I'd get the impulse to go play outside or go watch television, so instead of taking the ten seconds to carefully put it in my designated folder, I'd just shove it into some random textbook, or crumple it into the bottom of my backpack, and poof. Never to be seen again. It was so incredibly frustrating, even back then, knowing I did the work but just couldn't fight the impulse to rush on to the next thing. So yes, absolutely, acting on impulse was basically the entire defining feature of my childhood.
Have you felt like your difficulties with focus and restlessness have significantly impacted your ability to maintain relationships or perform daily tasks?

Well, yes, absolutely, and it’s—it’s really exactly what I was getting at earlier when I was talking about the toll this takes on my life. It bleeds into absolutely everything, every single relationship, every daily task you can think of. I mean, going back to what I said about losing the structure of my old job... that was really the linchpin for me, you know? In IT, especially when you've been doing it as long as I have, you rely on a certain rhythm, a certain framework provided by the company to keep you on track. And since I lost that structure, my reputation has just taken such a real, catastrophic hit. It's embarrassing, frankly. 

When you ask about daily tasks and relationships... well, professionally, my relationships are crumbling. I’ve lost those freelance clients I mentioned because I just couldn't focus enough to sit down and finish their daily troubleshooting requests or routine maintenance. I’d get restless, walk away from the computer to get a cup of coffee, and entirely forget what they had even asked me to do. And missing out on that senior service-manager role? That was a direct result of not being able to manage the daily, mundane tasks required to just get the documentation together. It’s a complete inability to execute the basic things that keep a career moving forward. 

And then, on a personal level, with relationships—my wife and I, it’s putting a massive, heavy strain on our marriage. Like I was saying before, we’ve had to worry about money so much lately, constantly sitting at the kitchen table trying to figure out how to cover the gaps because my income has become so unpredictable. And the root of all that financial worry, all that tension sitting right there between us, is that people just don’t trust me to follow through anymore. My clients don't trust me, the hiring managers don't trust me, and honestly, it’s getting to the point where it's hard for my own wife to trust me with the daily household tasks, too. If she asks me to pay a utility bill or call the plumber, she knows there's a very good chance I'll get distracted by something else and completely blow it. So, yes, it is impacting everything. Every single day is just a minefield of things I can't seem to get done, and it's pushing everyone away.
Did your difficulties with focus and restlessness significantly improve at any point in your life, or have they been relatively consistent since childhood?

Well, it’s—it’s a bit of a paradox, really, if I’m being completely honest about it. Because the underlying traits, the actual buzzing in my head and the constant need to move, that never really went away. Like I was just saying, it’s been there since Mrs. Gable’s third-grade class. But if you’re asking if it was always this... this destructive? No, it wasn't. There was a long period where things were actually okay, but it wasn't because my brain magically got better, it was because of the environment I was in. 

You see, working in IT support, especially at the enterprise level, you are entirely beholden to the ticketing system. Your entire day is structured for you by a computer program. A user submits a request, it pops up on your screen, you go fix the server or reset the credentials, you log your notes, and you close it. It’s an external framework. So for decades, I had this incredibly rigid scaffolding holding me up. I was still the guy bouncing his leg under the desk, sure, but I was highly functional. I even managed to get through my graduate degree because the syllabus provided that same kind of external, do-or-die deadline pressure. 

But the absolute bottom falling out... the point where it turned into this massive, life-ruining problem that we've been talking about? That is very easy to pinpoint. This has been causing serious, undeniable trouble for about 1 year and 10 months now. That’s exactly how long it’s been since I was fired from my last staff position. 

The day they let me go, I lost all of it. I lost the ticketing software, the daily stand-up meetings, the project managers breathing down my neck—I completely lost the systems that used to keep me on track. And without that external structure forcing me to focus and dictating my next move, it’s like my ability to function just evaporated into thin air. I’ve been in total freefall for a year and 10 months because I simply cannot replicate that structure on my own for this freelance stuff. I sit down at my desk at home, and without a system telling me what to do, my brain just scatters in a hundred different directions. So, the restlessness is lifelong, yes, but this complete inability to hold my life together? That started exactly 22 months ago, the day I lost my job and my systems.
Did you experience significant symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity prior to the age of 12?

Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, I know I kind of jumped the gun and went into all of this a bit already when we were talking about impulsivity earlier, but yes, definitely way before I was twelve. 

Like I mentioned with my mother... it’s practically a family legend at this point. She still brings it up, still jokes about those old grade school report cards to anyone who will listen. And it’s funny because, you know, when you're a kid, you don't really understand why you're doing what you're doing. You just know what the teachers are writing home to your parents. And every single year, it was the exact same chorus. They always made a point to write that I was a bright kid, which, honestly, almost made it worse, you know? Because if they think you're bright, they expect you to just naturally be able to *do* the basic things you're supposed to do. 

But then the rest of the report card would just be this absolute litany of complaints. That I never stayed in my seat—which, like I said, was just me wandering off without even realizing I was doing it—and that I constantly blurted out answers before anyone else could even think. And the homework... God, the homework. That was probably the most frustrating part for my parents, and for me, really. Because I would actually do it! I would sit there at the kitchen table and finish the math worksheets or the spelling sentences, but then I'd just lose it. I'd lose it on the way to school, or it would vanish into the black hole of my backpack or my desk, even when I had literally just done the work the night before. 

So, yes, to answer your question, long before I was twelve, all of that was already in full swing. It’s just... it’s always been there, just woven into who I was, long before I ever had to worry about IT careers or ticketing systems or mortgages. It was just me being the "bright but exhausting" kid, day in and day out.
Have you experienced significant difficulties with focus, restlessness, or impulsivity consistently throughout your adult life?

Well, I suppose it really depends on how we're defining "significant difficulties," because I feel like I kind of just touched on this a moment ago, right? The actual feelings—the restlessness, the static in my head, the feeling like my brain is a television flipping through channels on its own—that has absolutely been a constant, every single day of my adult life. I mean, from my twenties right through to now, in my fifties, I've always been the guy in the office tapping his pen on the desk, or pacing around the server room, or getting up to grab my fourth cup of coffee just because I physically couldn't sit still in my chair for another second. That internal motor just never, ever shuts off. 

But if you're asking if it was constantly ruining my life the way it is right now? Then, no, I wouldn't say the actual *difficulties* were consistent. And that goes right back to what I was just saying about the scaffolding of my old jobs. For decades, I was actually highly functional on paper. I got through my graduate degree, I climbed the ladder in enterprise IT, I was providing for my wife... but it was only because I had those incredibly rigid systems telling me exactly what to focus on and when. 

And honestly, looking back, it took a massive amount of energy to operate like that. I would come home at the end of the day just completely, utterly depleted from the sheer effort of forcing myself to stay on track, trying to channel all that restless, bouncing energy into the ticketing software so I wouldn't get fired. It was exhausting. 

So, the traits themselves? Yes, absolutely consistent. I've never known a day in my adult life where my brain was just quiet and focused. But the massive, life-altering difficulties... the part where I'm dropping the ball on every freelance client and straining my marriage because I can't focus long enough to pay a utility bill... that really only exploded when I lost that external structure a year and 10 months ago. It's like... the fire was always burning in the fireplace, consistently, for my whole adult life, but it didn't actually burn the entire house down until the systems were gone. Does that make sense?
Have you ever had a period of at least two months as an adult where you did not experience any symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity?

No, no, definitely not. I mean—two months? I don't think I've had two *days* where things were completely quiet up here, let alone two whole months. 

Like I was trying to explain just a second ago, the... the underlying current of it all, that constant hum in my head, it never takes a break. It never takes a vacation. And actually, speaking of vacations, that's probably the perfect example of what I mean. Because you'd think, right? You'd think if you step away from the stress of the office and the project managers, maybe your brain would just finally settle down and give you some peace. 

But my wife and I, we took this trip to the Outer Banks a few years back. It was supposed to be this incredibly relaxing getaway. And she can just sit there on a beach towel, totally engrossed in a paperback for three hours straight, not a care in the world. And me? I’m... I’m up after five minutes. I’m readjusting the beach umbrella, I’m walking down to the water, I’m coming back, I’m tapping my fingers on the cooler, I’m worrying about a patch update that was supposed to run on the mail server back home. I just physically and mentally cannot turn it off. Even when there is absolutely nothing I’m supposed to be focusing on, even when the only goal of the day is to relax, my brain is still just wildly flipping through those channels and my body feels like it needs to be doing something, anything, else. 

So, no. To have an entire sixty days where I wasn't feeling restless or where my thoughts weren't scattering everywhere? I honestly can't even fathom what that would feel like. It’s just always on. Every single day, year in and year out, regardless of whether I'm having a good month or a bad month, it's just always running in the background.
Have you experienced significant symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity for the majority of your adult life?

Well, I feel like we might be going in circles just a little bit here, or maybe I'm just not explaining it right, because like I was trying to say a few minutes ago... if we are specifically talking about the part where it's causing *serious* trouble? The kind of significant trouble that completely derails your life? Then no, that hasn't been the majority of my adult life at all. 

That level of absolute chaos has been going on for exactly one year and ten months. 

I know the exact timeframe because, well, that’s when I was fired. And I really don't mean to keep harping on about my old job, but you have to understand how crucial it was. For decades, I had this massive, built-in scaffolding. I had the enterprise IT ticketing systems, I had service level agreements, I had project managers literally standing over my cubicle asking for updates. It was exhausting to keep up with, yes, but it was a structure that basically forced me to stay on track. It was like... like I was bowling, but I had the bumper rails up. I might bounce wildly from side to side, but the system made sure I eventually hit the pins. 

But one year and ten months ago, they let me go. And overnight, all of that external structure, all those guardrails, they just vanished. And that is exactly when the real, serious trouble started. Because suddenly, I’m sitting at home in my home office, trying to piece together freelance contracts, and there is no ticketing system. There's no manager breathing down my neck. It’s just me and my own brain trying to regulate my day, and I quickly found out that without those systems that used to keep me on track... I just can't do it. I absolutely cannot do it. 

So, the restlessness and the noise in my head? Sure, that's been my whole adult life. But the significant symptoms actually ruining my livelihood and causing this severe level of trouble? That is strictly a product of the last year and ten months, ever since I lost that job and all the systems that went with it.
Have you experienced difficulties with focus, restlessness, or impulsivity in multiple areas of your life, such as at work, at home, or in social situations?
